newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Argentina downplays Mercosur rift with Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Argentina downplays Mercosur rift with Brazil.

text.p: Hoping to douse talk of a rift in Mercosur, a high-level Argentine official on Thursday downplayed Buenos Aires' complaints about Brazilian trade policy.
"The Argentine government is not the least bit concerned about the trade balance with Brazil," Alieto Guadagni, Argentina's Trade, Industry and Mining Secretary, told reporters.
He said trade between the two biggest members of the four-nation Mercosur customs union should reach a point close to equilibrium by the end of the year.

Guadagni's comments came after two days of talks with seniro Brazilian officials, including Finance Minister Pedro Malan, reportedly to complain that Brazil was dragging its feet in the implementation of Mercosur rules.

The complaints, ranging from export subsidies to financial restrictions, were reportedly sparked by Argentina's shrinking trade surplus with Brazil to $6 million in August from an average monthly gap of around $100 million over the last year.
Trade between the two countries totalled $9.6 billion in 1995, with Argentina enjoying a trade surplus of $1.13 billion for the year.
Guadagni, a former ambassador to Brazil, flew to Brasilia on Monday packing a laundry list of complaints, ranging from export subsidies to financial restrictions, according to diplomats.
The Brazilian press on Wednesday blasted Argentina, saying it was blaming its own economic woes on Brazil's Mercosur trade policy.
"The problem is not here; it's there," O Estado de Sao Paulo daily said in an editorial.
On Thursday morning, Guadagni dismissed reports Buenos Aires was upset about the trend in imports and exports, saying the important thing is that trade between the two countries continue to grow.
"We're going to see a period of joint growth in the two economies" once Argentina shakes off recession, he said. "From now on, we're going to see equal (trade) flows."
Rather, he stressed the need for Mercosur members to coordinate efforts designed to draw investment to the region.
Guadagni said an ongoing fiscal war between Brazil's states competing to attract foreign investors threatens to hurt Mercosur members.
Incentives should not upset the "natural process of specific advantages" offered by each partner. Mercosur also includes Paraguay and Uruguay and Chile is an associate.
Guadagni also said his government was concerned over the problems two Argentine banks are having entering the Brazilian market.
